design application. Sixty participants evaluated three each of urban, waterfront, and green environments using
virtual reality technology. The audio-visual characteristics of environments were quantified, and environmental
perception was assessed per 14 audio-visual element identifications, six perceived affective qualities, and six
overall environmental qualities. The restoration responses were classified as psychological and physiological.
Accordingly, 10 restoration models that can interpret design factors of the urban environment with a maximum
correlation of 0.80 and an explanatory power of 22 % emerged from urban audio-visual design elements and
psycho-physiological responses. Consequently, to improve restoration response, visually attractive and spatial-
natural landscapes and acoustically supportive and tranquil soundscapes should be created. Moreover, urban
designers can use the models to clearly identify physical characteristics that should be prioritized when pro-
moting the health improvement of urbanites. Furthermore, the study findings can serve as basic data for the
development of healthy environments.

3.3. Restoration model based on audio-visual interactions in various
environments
To propose a restoration model from the perspective of audio-visual
interaction, CCA was performed to investigate the relationships of
psycho-physiological responses to physical characteristics and environ-
mental perception. Through CCA analysis, the study derived the primary
model with the greatest correlation between psycho-physiological
response, physical characteristics, and environmental perception, after which an additional canonical variate model revealed a strong correla-
tion while being independent of model 1. This process was repeated, and
only models evaluated to be statistically significant were presented in
Fig. 6 and Table 3 (p-value <0.05). For each model, the corresponding
proportions of variation are summarized in Table 3. Canonical loadings
are shown in Fig. 6. For a clear understanding of the CCA results, the
findings were interpreted by focusing on the variables with a canonical loading of 0.5 or higher.
3.3.1. Relationship between physical characteristics and psycho-
physiological restoration
As shown in Fig. 6 (a), there was a strong correlation (0.80) between
the physical characteristics and psychological restoration factors.
Among the physical characteristics factors, LAeq (sound strength), LA5-
A95 (temporal variation), loudness, water ratio, and grey ratio were
identified as important, while among the psychological restoration
factors, “escaping to,” valence, fascination, arousal, and negative affect
were similarly identified. As LAeq, LA5-A95, and loudness decreased in an
auditory environment and as the grey ratio decreased and water ratio
increased in a visual environment, psychological facets of fascination,
“breaking away,” and valence increased, and arousal and negative affect
were reduced. Regarding explanatory power, 29 % of the variance in the
psychological restoration was explained by the set of canonical variables
for the factor, and 19 % by physical characteristics. The correlation between physical characteristics and physiological restoration was not
significant and, thus, not presented (p =0.982).

restoration

factor and the psycho-physiological restoration factor is shown in Fig. 6 (b)–(c). The correlation between the factors was 0.78, as can be seen in
Fig. 6 (b). Of the facets of psychological restoration, “breaking away,”
valence, fascination, and “escaping to” increased. Of the emotional
facets, arousal, and negative affect decreased. Meanwhile, the audio-
visual elements like artifact-related (traffic noise, music, vehicle, and
building) and human-related (human sound and people) elements

audio-visual elements were also low—all under 0.5. The explanatory

Appendix A. Audio-visual data collection method and laboratory experiment set-up with virtual reality techniques
To create an evaluation environment that could be confined to a laboratory, audio-visual data were collected at each of the sites. Data from the nine
sites were collected under the same conditions: daytime (10 am–2 pm) in May 2020 when the weather was clear and warm—the average temperature
of 20.6◦C degrees. Visual data were recorded in high resolution (8k) using a six-channel 360 camera (Insta 360 pro, Insta 360). Auditory data were
recorded by connecting a four-channel ambisonic microphone (Soundfield SPS 200, Sound field Ltd.) to a portable sound recorder (Mixpre-6, Sound
devices) with an ambisonic set-up of A-formant first-order (FOA). To minimize wind noise in audio recordings, a microphone windshield was used. To
calibrate the evaluation environment in the laboratory setting to the identical sound pressure level (SPL) in the field, simultaneous recordings were
made using an additional microphone (half-inch microphone, AE 46, GRAS Sound and Vibration) that was connected to another portable sound
recorder (AS-70, RION) (See the Fig. A.1). The camera and the microphones were all mounted on a tripod positioned in a fixed location, and all
recordings were made at the average human eye level of 1.6 meters for three minutes. To synchronize the visual and auditory recordings, a clapping
motion and sound were used at the start of each recording.
VR technology was used to create an evaluation environment in the laboratory, similar to the field, simulating this environment using Unity 3D
software. The ecological validity of this technology in environmental evaluation has been confirmed in previous studies (Hong et al., 2019; Maffei,
Masullo, Pascale, Ruggiero, & Romero, 2015).
The six-channel videos were edited to 360◦images using stitching software (Insta 360 pro stitcher), and the edited visual information was pre-
sented to the participants via an HMD (VIVE Pro Eye, HTC). The four-channel sound sources were converted from A-format to B-format FOA using
ambisonic plug-ins (sound devices), and the output was downmixed to binaural, by Spatial audio SDK (Spatial Audio ALI, Google) built in Unity 3D
software. The participants received edited auditory information through an open-type headphone (HD-650, Sennheiser). Sound orientation was
implemented in real-time, according to the changing head position of the participants turning their heads, by using a tracker built into the HMD. To
adjust the sound of the VR environment to the SPL of actual locations, nine binaural sound sources were recorded using a head and torso simulator
(Type 4100, Brüel & Kjær). The average SPL of the two-channel sound sources was adjusted, to match the average SPL of the sound in the field (LAeq),
by using Adobe Audition software (version 1.5, Adobe). All stimuli were edited to last three minutes.

Appendix B. Physical characteristics of the audio-visual stimulus
The physical characteristics of the on-site audio-visual environment were classified as acoustic or visual parameters and were quantified as shown
in Table B.1. Acoustic parameters included sound strength (LAeq), spectral contents (LCeq-Aeq), temporal variation (LA5-A95), and psychoacoustics
(loudness and sharpness). LAeq indicated A-weighted equivalent continuous sound pressure levels. LCeq-Aeq was defined as the difference between C-
weight SPL and A-weight SPL, while LA5-A95 was the difference between the 5th and 95th percentile sound pressure levels. Loudness referred to the
subjective perception of sound pressure strongly associated with SPL. Sharpness was determined based on the distribution of a sound’s high- and low
frequencies, for a specific value of loudness. The impact of a high-frequency spectrum causes rising sharpness with increasing volume. The impact
analysis was performed using dBFA32 software (01 dB) and SQT Sound Quality software (PULSE, Brüel & Kjær). among visual parameters, the color
ratio was analyzed for green, water, sky, and grey, representing vegetation (e.g., tree, forest, and grass), waterfront (e.g., river, ocean, water and
fountain), sky, and artifacts (e.g., building, road, and vehicle), respectively, through the following steps. First, 3D videos were converted to 2D images.
The researchers then used Photoshop to manually divide the outer boundary for each visual factor. As in Fig. B.1, each segmented object was assigned
a layer for further differentiation and segmentation. Thus, to avoid potential errors from algorithm-based image segmentation techniques, the re-
searchers separated the objects personally. Next, an image color summarizer (Krzywinski, 2003) computed the ratio of a segment to the entire pixel
area, and these ratios were added for each of the green, water, sky, and grey elements. Luminance was also analyzed (Puyana-Romero, Ciaburro,
Brambilla, Garzo´n, & Maffei, 2019) by computing an RGB ratio on unsegmented 2D images, as shown in Fig. B.1, using the image color summarizer.
Subsequently, the standard luminance formula computed the luminance (International Telecommunications Union, 2011) - 0.299 × red + 0.587 ×
green + 0.114 × blue.

Appendix D. Detailed account of the experimental procedure
On Day 1, psycho-physiological responses were measured as follows. When the participants arrived at the laboratory, a short session was con-
ducted to explain the previously distributed written documents to aid them in fully understanding the questionnaire items. Subsequently, the par-
ticipants put on the VR devices (HMD and headphones) and the hardware for measuring physiological responses (HRV and EEG) (See the Fig. D.1). The
functioning of the devices and any signal interference were checked while the participants were wearing them. For participants unfamiliar with VR
devices, a brief training session (e.g., how to choose an answer to a question, how to submit an answer, and how to replay a stimulus) was provided to
acclimatize them to the evaluation environment.
Once all preparations were completed, the participants rested for a short while to make themselves comfortable, and their physiological responses
in a resting state were measured. These measurements in a resting state were used as a reference to compare the physiological responses to the urban,
waterfront, and green space experiences. The comparison between the state of stimulus and no stimulus (an environment with a black background and

Appendix E. Questionnaires
First, the category of individual characteristics comprised items regarding the state of their health and those regarding demographic character-
istics, including a simple question regarding gender. The state of their health was assessed with 1) the perceived stress scale, a scale assessing the
subjective stress level in everyday life, and 2) items regarding sensitivity to noise. Demographic characteristics were assessed with 1) the Temper-
ament and Character Inventory (Revised Short Version), a scale to assess character and temperament, 2) the World Health Organization Quality of Life
(Brief Version), a scale to assess life satisfaction, and 3) the Urban Residents Psychological Security scale, a scale to assess psychological security in an
urban environment typically experienced by urbanite participants.
Next, to examine the psychological restoration response, the second category consisted of 1) the Perceived Restorativeness Soundscape Scale
(PRSS), developed based on ART to assess the restorative effect of soundscape in six domains: fascination, “breaking away,”, “escaping to,”
compatibility, coherence, and scope, 2) the Self-Assessment Manikin (SAM), a scale to assess affective response to stimuli in three domains: valence,
arousal, and dominance, and 3) the Positive Affect and Negative Affect Scale (PANAS), to assess mood state in the two dimensions of positive and
negative affect. Two different affective scales were used because the PANAS is a verbal assessment tool and accordingly, individuals may have
different interpretations based on emotional and cultural differences in nuance and intensity. By contrast, the SAM is a pictorial assessment tool and
can thus be used to control the difference in responses due to the use of words.
Lastly, the perception of the audio-visual environment was assessed separately for soundscape and landscape. Regarding the evaluation of
soundscapes, within the large framework of the ISO 12,913–2 (Hotelling, 1935) protocols, the following items were used: 1) sound source identifi-
cation (traffic noise, other noise, human sound, music, birdsong, water sound, wind sound), 2) 14 semantic expressions (pleasant, vibrant, eventful,
informative, annoying, stressful, chaotic, artificial, uninformative, calm, relaxing, natural, monotonous, uneventful) to assess the perceived affective
quality of soundscape, and 3) overall impression, appropriateness, and sound satisfaction concerning overall environmental quality. Landscapes were
evaluated using the same method as for soundscapes, as follows: 1) visual elements (vehicle, building, people, open space, vegetation, water, sky), 2)
14 semantic attributes (appealing, harmonious, orderly, repulsive, disharmonious, disorderly, complex, simple, open, natural, wide, enclosed, arti-
ficial, narrow) to assess the perceived affective quality of the landscape, and 3) scenic beauty, the status of infrastructures, and visual satisfaction

Appendix F. Principal component analysis of perceived affective quality
A principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on the responses to the 14 semantic expressions to extract the dimensions of the soundscape
and landscape perception before interpreting the perceived affective quality. The PCA results are summarized in Table F.1. All Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin
measures of sampling adequacy were over 0.8, suggesting that the sample was adequate and the results of Bartlett’s test of sphericity were signifi-
cant (p<0.01). Three dimensions were extracted for soundscape perception: supportive soundscape (16.27 %), detrimental soundscape (29.27 %), and
tranquil soundscape (28.15 %). The supportive soundscape was labeled Factor 1, based on the high factor loadings of attributes like vibrant and pleasant,
and the detrimental soundscape was labeled Factor 2, based on the high factor loadings of negative attributes such as annoying and stressful. The
tranquil soundscape was labeled as Factor 3, based on high factor loadings for monotonous and calm. Three dimensions of landscape perception were
extracted: attractive landscape (19.25 %), discomforting landscape (21.44 %), and spatial/natural landscape (21.83 %). The Attractive landscape was
labeled Factor 1, given the high factor loadings of orderly, appealing, and harmonious, and the discomforting landscape as Factor 2, given the high
factor loadings of disharmonious and repulsive. Similarly, the spatial and natural landscape was labeled Factor 3, with high factor loadings of simple,
open, natural, and wide.
The factor scores were computed using the extracted soundscape and landscape dimensions. Factor score is a numerical value of a variable that
